Hon. P. J. A. CARDIN (Minister of Public Works) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to authorize the Minister of Public Works, on behalf of His Majesty, to enter into an agreement with the corporation of the city of Ottawa to extend the period of the existing agreement with the corporation for one year from 1st July, 1935.
What is it all about?

In the year 1920 an agreement was made between the then Minister of Public Works and the city of Ottawa by which the dominion government was to pay to the city of Ottawa the sum of $75,000 to compensate for all claims of the city in connection with the sprinkling of certain streets, which was to be undertaken by the federal government, and also for fire protection. After a long discussion between representatives of the city and the Minister of Public Works it was agreed that the federal government should pay the sum of $75,000 in settlement of all claims that the city might have against it. The agreement was renewed each year, and in 1925 the amount of $75,000 was increased to $100,000. Since that time the agreement has been renewed every
City of Ottawa Agreement

year. The object of the bill to be introduced is to authorize the Minister of Public Works to extend the agreement for another year.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Young in the chair.
Would the minister inform the committee on what basis the $100,000 was arrived at as a fair and equitable amount?

I cannot give the hon. member exact details as to the claim put in by the city. If I remember correctly, the amount claimed by the city in respect of various items amounted to about $200,000, and it was as a result of a compromise between the Minister of Public Works and the city that the amount was reduced to the sum of $75,000. As a result of that agreement the city of Ottawa agreed to abandon all claims it had made up to that time.
I understood the minister to say that-the amount of $100,000 was for all claims.
No; in the first instance it was $75,000.
The amount of $75,000 for all claims against the government. Now I understand it is an annual claim.
It has always been an annual claim.
Is this $100,000 for fire protection and' other services rendered to the federal buildings in Ottawa?
Yes

I should like to have some idea as to how the figure is arrived at. It may be too high or it may be too low. I think there ought to be some explanation as to how the amount is made up. Perhaps the minister would be able to inform the committee as to the value of buildings owned by the government in Ottawa, and with that information we might have some idea as to what the service is worth, on the ordinary assessed value.

I confess that I cannot give in detail what the hon. member is asking. I am not ready to admit that the claim made by the city of Ottawa at the time of the agreement was entirely justified. Numerous items were mentioned by the city, and the amount was strongly objected to by the then minister. It was as a result of a mutual understanding that the agreement was reached, and there is no real or definite basis upon which the amount of $75,000 has been agreed upon. It was a matter of agreement.
The hon. member wants to know what we get for our money.

We get fire protection for all our buildings, and it is compensation, too, for the water used for sprinkling certain streets, for which the federal government is responsible. At the same time there is something to take the place of the taxes the federal government is not paying on properties in Ottawa.

I believe the federal government gets the same concessions in all municipalities; they do not pay taxes on federal properties. I do not think other municipalities are receiving the same treatment as is the city of Ottawa, and if the government is paying to Ottawa something in lieu of taxes, may I say that other cities in Canada might come to the government expecting the same treatment. It is quite true that in 1920 the government may have made an agreement for $75,000. The minister claims that he does not know whether the sum was equitable or otherwise. At any rate it appears that in 1925 another government of which the minister may have been a member increased the grant to $100,000. If the amount was not equitable in 1920 I cannot understand why it was increased by $25,000 or 33J per cent just a few years later. I am not going to press the point just now, but when the bill is in committee I would ask the minister to give the details which we ought to have on a measure of this kind.
Resolution reported, read the second time and concurred in. Mr. Cardin thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 54, to authoriz-e an agreement between His Majesty the King and the corporation of the city of Ottawa.

The agreement was dated
March 13, 1920, and these were the items which were the basis of the claim of the city of Ottawa against the federal government. Claims have been pressed on many occasions by the city and were resisted by the federal government for a long time, but in the end it was decided that it would be advantageous for both parties if an agreement were reached, and after long discussions it was agreed in 1920 that the sum of $75,000 should be paid every year to the city of Ottawa to compensate it for its fire protection of all the public buildings in Ottawa, for street sprinkling, and in lieu of the taxes that would ordinarily be assessed on private property.
My hon. friend from Winnipeg North (Mr. Heaps) said that if we applied this principle in the city of Ottawa we should apply it elsewhere, but Ottawa is in a different position from any other city where we have only one or two public buildings, and all governments in the past have felt that they should be a little more generous to the capital which we are all interested in developing and beautifying so that it will be an attraction to visitors to our country. I admit that a certain amount of sentiment may have entered into the decision which was reached by the government in 1920, but I believe that the contribution we are making to the city of Ottawa is justified. It has been continued by all governments since 1920, and the bill presently before the committee provides for an extension of the agreement for one year, which otherwise would lapse on the first of July next.

The principle has been
established and has been in effect now for sixteen years, and I do not think it is likely that we will go back on it. I do not think that parliament has dealt ungenerously with the city of Ottawa. I think as a rule it has dealt with it pretty fairly. I myself would not like to deal unfairly with the city of Ottawa, but I remember that only a few years ago when parliament appropriated money for a confederation park, running into many millions of dollars, the people of Ottawa did not seem to appreciate the gift which parliament was making to the city, and after the land had been expropriated and millions of dollars spent a demand was made upon the government that it should compensate the city for the taxes which had been lost through the demolishing of the buildings that had been torn down for the park, and the wiping out of that source of city revenue. I want to point out that the principle is exactly the same in other cities where you have public buildings. The municipalities there have to provide fire equipment, police protection, water service and every other service that a municipality gives; to public buildings. While we may have-only one federal capital we have nine provincial capitals, and in many of them, if not in all, we find quite a large number of buildings which are not paying taxes to their respective municipalities.
While I want to deal fairly with Ottawa, while I am not opposing this grant of $100,000 proposed by the present bill, I still think the information given by the minister is not adequate. I feel that the particulars he gave of the various items submitted in 1920 verged almost on the grotesque. They asked for $57,000 in lieu of the taxes that were not being paid by the federal government. Evidently they tried to put these as high as possible when they expressed the pious hope that they should receive $870,000, but they were willing to settle for less than ten cents on the dollar. Even at that, they -must have felt they got a pretty good bargain. I think we should have some idea as to what we receive in return for the $100,000 granted. All I am able to find out from the minister is that this amount is given to the municipal authorities for fire protection. It cannot be for police protection as the government polices its own buildings. It is in lieu of the general taxation which the private citizen is compelled to pay the municipalities. All I can point out in this regard is that in practically every provincial capital there are either federal or

If the Minister of Public Works is asked to give the same treatment to other municipalities that he has given to Ottawa for a number of years, I hope he will give them the same sympathetic consideration.

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO FEES, CHARGES AND ROYALTIES AND TO CONSTITUTE A COPYRIGHT APPEAL BOARD

speechtext:
Hon. FERNAND RINFRET (Secretary of State) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution :
That it is expedient to bring in a measure to amend the Copyright Amendment Act, 1931, with respect to fees, charges and royalties which may be collected, and to provide for the constitution of a copyright appeal board and for the travelling and living expenses of the members thereof, and for the remuneration and travelling and living expenses of persons appearing before the board in an advisory capacity.
He said: This resolution precedes a bill to which I referred when we were discussing the bill introduced by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Esling). The bill to be introduced is based upon a report which was filed with the present government on October 29 by His Honour Judge Parker, a commissioner appointed under the Inquiries Act, to inquire into the copyright situation and especially that created by the exacting of fees by the Canadian Performing Right Society Limited. I may say that the inquiry dealt mostly with section 10 of the Copyright Amendment Act, 1931, which stipulates:
Each association, society or company which carries on in Canada the business of acquiring copyrights of dramatico-musical or musical works or of performing rights therein, and which deals with or in the issue or grant of licences for the performance in Canada of dramatico-musical or musical works in which copyright subsists, shall, from time to time, file with the minister at the copyright office-
Then follow particulars of the lists of works to be filed and the statements of fees, charges and royalties. In 1935 this act was still further amended by the then Secretary of State (Mr. Cahan). This amendment stated that when in the opinion of the minister a society was charging excessive fees with respect to copyright such as I have just mentioned, a commissioner might be appointed

to inquire into and report on such matters. On March 22, 1935, His Honour James Parker was appointed by the former government to inquire into a situation created by the exacting of fees by the Canadian Performing Right Society Limited and any other society which had unduly withheld the issue or granting of licences with respect to the performance of musical works in Canada. This report has been referred to before and I mentioned it when discussing the bill introduced by the hon. member for Kootenay West. In his report Judge Parker passes judgment upon a list of fees filed by the Canadian Performing Right Society and has recommended that other fees would represent more fairly what the performing rights were worth. The commissioner also recommended certain amendments to the Copyright Act. His recommendations are contained in three paragraphs at the end of his report. The first recommendation is:
That there be included in the Canadian Copyright Act a clause similar to section 40 of the Patent Act, to prevent vexatious and unwarranted legal proceedings.
This is section 66 of the Consolidated Patent Act. His next recommendation was that section 17 of the Copyright Act be amended. This section defines the performance of a musical work by a church, college or school or by a religious, charitable or fraternal organization, provided such performance is given without private profit. There was some confusion as to what was meant by private profit and Judge Parker has recommended that the act be amended to more clearly define this term. His third recommendation was:
That the Copyright Act as amended so as to provide for the establishment of an appeal tribunal, to determine disputes arising out of performance in public and to approve of the tariffs of the Canadian Performing Right Society Limited from time to time before they become effective.
I may say that at this late hour I do not think it would be advisable to enter into a detailed discussion of these amendments. My suggestion would be rather that if this resolution were passed I could introduce a bill which would afford every hon. member an opportunity to ascertain exactly what is proposed in the legislation.
It is not the intention to establish a permanent tribunal in the sense that it would sit all the year or that it would constitute some kind of new commission added to the long list of commissions we already have. But basing our bill upon legislation introduced in another country, what we propose to do is this: We want such societies as I have

Copyright Act-Mr. Bennett
mentioned to file their fees on the first day of November of each year; then, allowing a certain number of days, not less than twenty-one, it would be open to all interested parties to file protests or representations concerning the fees, and in the course of December; thereafter the tribunal would sit, and in my opinion in two or three weeks at most it would pronounce upon these disputes.
The intention is to have the tribunal appointed during pleasure. It will include a member of the judiciary, preferably a judge of the exchequer court. But in order to obviate the necessity of coming back to parliament from time to time to amend the bill, it is simply intended that the chairman of the commission shall be a member of the high judiciary, the other members of the commission being two officers of the public service. There again no special mention is made, but the intention is that one might be from the copyright office and the other from the Department of Justice.

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO FEES, CHARGES AND ROYALTIES AND TO CONSTITUTE A COPYRIGHT APPEAL BOARD
speechtext: Would this commission have power to fix fees.

subtopic: AMENDMENT WITH RESPECT TO FEES, CHARGES AND ROYALTIES AND TO CONSTITUTE A COPYRIGHT APPEAL BOARD
speechtext:
Yes, this commission will pronounce on fees; that is the recommendation and that is the intention. It is not intended to give any remuneration to any of the three commissioners, one being a judge and the others members of the public service, but they may have to travel and would have to be allowed living and travelling expenses. It might also develop that in certain years the department might feel that legal advice should be submitted to the commission and that is why the bill which I shall introduce is preceded by this resolution.
If the house would accept the agreement that the discussion, even on the principle of the bill, might be reserved until the second reading, and does not object to the resolution in its present form, I would ask that the resolution be passed in committee so as to allow me to introduce the bill and so that everyone would know what is in it. It is not the intention of the government to recommend any extensive amendment to the Copyright Act. As I stated the other day, there will be this fall a meeting in Brussels of the International Union on Copyright and the whole matter of copyright will then be considered; but it is not possible to delay this bill any further, because, in the first place, the dealings of the Canadian Performing Right Society and such associations have not so far been foreseen by any preceding international convention on copyright, and because,
in the second place, in the amendment of 1935 the then Secretary of State had the house adopt a bill whereby all litigation was suspended during the inquiry by Judge Parker. I have had to extend further the time of suspension of all such litigation, as provided for in the 1935 amendment, until this house shall have taken action. I may point out, however, that not only is it desirable to appoint an appeal tribunal which will sit in December, 1936, but it is also necessary to give the Secretary of State power to apply the rates recommended by Judge Parker not only for the time intervening between the filing of his report and the operation of this new tribunal but also for the transition stage between the time he was appointed and the time he made his report. After consultation with the Department of Justice I have been advised that there is doubt as to whether the Secretary of State would have the right to make that adjustment unless he were authorized by parliament. For all these reasons I commend the resolution to the house and, on the understanding I have just given, perhaps the house will allow the resolution to go through committee so that I may introduce the bill which is to be based upon it.

I need only point out that there are two matters which are affected; one is our obligations under the Berne convention to which we became a party during the regime, I believe, of the government of which
Bank oj Canada-Ruling

the Secretary of State was a member and which is binding upon us, and the second is the extent to which we are warranted in setting up another commission to deal with a matter of this kind. As to the first, ample opportunity will be afforded when the bill is in committee to discuss it if the minister is agreeable to that, because it is a matter in which we have incurred international obligations that are not easily set at nought. On the second point, I had thought that possibly this matter could be referred to the board of railway commissioners. They have not been too busy. They have been accustomed to fixing freight rates and might easily deal with a problem of this kind, because they would approach it without preconceived notions, and the law requires them to have certain qualifications. Moreover, they represent every part of Canada and they would bring to bear upon the matter before them a wealth of experience that could not be expected from officials of departments in matters of this sort, and this would save a lot of cost. However, that matter can possibly be discussed later. I have no desire to impede the hon. gentleman in getting his resolution into committee, but we must reserve our rights to have questions asked and answered when the bill itself is in committee of the whole if the resolution is given effect to to-night.
